newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK handover sets stage for Taiwan-China unity talk.
newsitem.headline: HK handover sets stage for Taiwan-China unity talk.

text.p: Hong Kong has invited Beijing's arch-rival Taiwan to celebrate the British colony's handover in two weeks' time, setting the stage for possible Taiwan-China reunification talks.
Diplomats predicted officials from Beijing and Taipei would confer on the sidelines of the gala despite strained ties and military exercises later this month.
Stephen Lam, the Hong Kong government's coordinator of the handover ceremonies, said 60 Taiwan officials had been invited.

"They are being invited in their personal capacities," Lam said. "As for seating arrangements...if you have done wedding banquets for two or three hundred people, you know how difficult it is, and now we are trying to do one for 4,000 people."

In Taipei, William Li, director of the Hong Kong and Macau affairs department of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, said: "We have approved Straits Exchange Foundation chairman Koo Chen-fu to attend the events."
No senior officials of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China were expected to attend.
Koo heads a semi-official agency that handles the Nationalist island's stalled contacts with Beijing.
Britain, China and the Hong Kong government have invited over 4,000 people to an end-of-empire gala banquet and handover ceremony straddling midnight June 30 and the morning of July 1.

Meanwhile, as preparations gathered pace, the end of Britain's empire was signalled by the removal on Monday of Queen Elizabeth's portrait from the officers' mess in the British garrison headquarters.

Larger-than-life photographs of the queen and her consort Prince Philip were taken down at the Prince of Wales Barracks and handed to the British Trade Commission which is to become London's consular and diplomatic mission after the withdrawal.

"Every British officers' mess in the world has portraits of the Queen and the Duke," said army Captain Sara Wood. "Taking these down was a part of the process of our preparing to leave Hong Kong. We were just happy to find a fitting home for them."
At the stroke of midnight, China will regain sovereignty over Hong Kong, ending 156 years of colonial rule which began with imperial China's humiliating defeat in the Opium Wars.
Britain's royal heir Prince Charles will hand back the territory to China's President Jiang Zemin.
Governor Chris Patten, British army troops, Royal Navy sailors and garrison staff will leave by sea and air in a final farewell to Britain's last imperial outpost in Asia.

China's late leader Deng Xiaoping devised a "one country two systems" policy for Hong Kong to keep its capitalist way of life for a further 50 years, to serve as a model for Taiwan's eventual reunification with the communist-ruled mainland.
Taiwan, which calls itself the Republic of China, is the vestige of the Nationalist government that ruled the mainland before 1949 when the communists won a long-drawn-out civil war.
In recent years Beijing and Taiwan have been sparring over what the mainland sees as provocative moves towards formal independence by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui.
Diplomats in Hong Kong said they expected Beijing-Taiwan talks in some shape or form to take place on the sidelines of the Hong Kong handover ceremonies.
China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen told the South China Morning Post Hong Kong must serve as a bridge to the world.
"China is going to continue economic development and reform, therefore we we still need Hong Kong as bridge and window."
He also signalled a hands-off approach to protests and press freedom in the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR, issues that the local government would be free to handle.
Many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people have fretted that China might impose communist style repression.
